slides.title: A number is not yet a measurement
keyPoints: The parcel rule accepts at most two grams.
The existing device returns integer milligrams.
A negative reading means failure, not a light parcel.
slides.narration: Imagine reviewing a parcel station after its supplier changes. The business rule still says that a sample may weigh at most two grams. The device supplies an integer, but that integer counts milligrams. A result of 1250 therefore means one and a quarter grams. The trouble is deeper than a different function name: a negative result means the device failed. Before drawing a class, write down the meaning of a successful value and the meaning of a failed call. Our job is to keep the parcel rule clear while honoring both parts of that contract. The device here is simulated; no hardware is contacted.
actions: Ask whether -1 should be accepted as a very light parcel.
Write the input unit and output unit before discussing types.

question.prompt: Why is renaming milligrams to grams insufficient?
question.answer: It changes the spelling without converting the unit or translating the negative failure convention.

slides.title: Begin with one honest conversion
keyPoints: Read one integer.
Reject the device error range.
Divide by 1000.0 to preserve the fraction.
slides.narration: For one caller, a small function solves this problem well. The input parameter is an integer value, so the function receives its own copy of that number. If the value is negative, throw stops the normal return path. Otherwise, the decimal point in 1000.0 makes the division use floating-point arithmetic. The result is a double, a type that can represent fractional values approximately. In this example, 1.25 is exactly representable. Notice what is absent: we do not need inheritance, an owning pointer, or a named pattern to explain this first version. Keep this version when every caller can simply use the function.
actions: Predict the two output lines.
Run the program, then change 1250 to 2001.

question.prompt: Does the helper need an object to remember the device?
question.answer: No. It receives one reading by value and has no stored connection or lifetime obligation.

slides.title: A cast after division repairs nothing
keyPoints: 1999 / 1000 is integer division.
Casting the result cannot restore lost digits.
A missing error check can approve failed hardware.
slides.narration: A type conversion can look careful while occurring too late. In bad_grams, the expression inside parentheses divides two integers first. That produces one for the reading 1999. The cast then turns that one into a double; the missing fraction is already gone. The second defect is different. Dividing a negative failure marker by a floating-point divisor preserves a negative value, and a comparison with two accepts it. Neither bug is a compiler error. Both expressions obey C++ rules while breaking the application contract. Our demonstration prints the wrong answers safely so that you can connect each symptom to its exact cause.
actions: Pause before running and predict lost and failure accepted.
Identify which bug needs a type fix and which needs a validation fix.

question.prompt: Why does static_cast<double>(1999 / 1000) produce 1 rather than 1.999?
question.answer: Integer division happens first. The later cast converts the already-truncated integer result.

slides.title: Now the caller needs a Scale
keyPoints: Existing rules accept const Scale&.
LegacyScale supplies milligrams(), not grams().
Translate once at the boundary.
slides.narration: Now add the requirement that makes the class useful. Several existing rules already accept a Scale reference. They expect a grams operation, and different devices may be chosen while the program runs. Our helper converts a number, but it does not make a LegacyScale usable through that object interface. An adapter is the small boundary object that fills this gap. ScaleAdapter presents the operation callers expect and uses the old service internally. We choose it to protect an existing agreement, not simply because a wrapper would be possible. Changing every caller would spread the device's units and errors throughout the application.
actions: Name the target, old service, translator, and client.
Ask which code should change when a new device API arrives.

question.prompt: Which code should know that negative milligrams means device failure?
question.answer: The device integration boundary, here ScaleAdapter, should translate that convention before application rules receive a measurement.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Accept an existing LegacyScale without changing its class.
Return fractional grams and reject every negative raw reading.
Accept exactly two grams and reject a heavier sample.
slides.narration:
A gram-based parcel rule. Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.

Accept an existing LegacyScale without changing its class. Return fractional grams and reject every negative raw reading. Accept exactly two grams and reject a heavier sample.

The adapter never owns or deletes device_. A successful grams call returns a nonnegative value in grams. Device failure never becomes a successful parcel decision. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A free conversion function is simpler if all callers can use it. A multiple-inheritance adapter can reuse protected legacy behavior but ties the adapter to a legacy base subobject and its construction rules.

comparisons.label: Chosen design
comparisons.text: Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.

comparisons.label: A reasonable alternative
comparisons.text: A free conversion function is simpler if all callers can use it. A multiple-inheritance adapter can reuse protected legacy behavior but ties the adapter to a legacy base subobject and its construction rules.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Adapter implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: The adapter never owns or deletes device_. A successful grams call returns a nonnegative value in grams. Device failure never becomes a successful parcel decision.

slides.title: The problem: one program, two meanings of weight
keyPoints: A parcel station decides whether a sample weighs at most two grams.
For one caller, the simplest reasonable answer is a direct conversion.
slides.narration:
A parcel station decides whether a sample weighs at most two grams. Its application already asks a Scale for grams. A replacement device is not available. The old device returns an integer count of milligrams through milligrams(), and a negative value means the device failed. We must reuse that device without teaching every parcel rule its old spelling, units, and error convention. The answer must preserve fractions: 1,250 milligrams means 1.25 grams.

For one caller, the simplest reasonable answer is a direct conversion. Read the integer, reject negative results, and divide by 1000.0. A helper function could keep that operation in one place. If every caller can use that helper, stop there. A class does not improve a problem that is already solved clearly. Our added constraint is different: existing rules accept a Scale reference and may receive several kinds of scales at run time.

question.prompt: What goes wrong if a parcel rule treats 1250 milligrams as 1250 grams?
question.answer: It compares different units and rejects a parcel that actually weighs 1.25 grams. Renaming a method is insufficient; the boundary must translate both the number and the device's error convention.

slides.title: The failure that calls for a translator
keyPoints: Passing LegacyScale straight to light_enough does not compile.
An adapter is an object that makes an existing service meet another interface.
slides.narration:
Passing LegacyScale straight to light_enough does not compile. It is not a Scale, and it has no grams member. Merely renaming milligrams would still leave the wrong unit and would treat a failure signal as a very light parcel. Changing every rule would mix device concerns with parcel rules. Each new device would repeat that work.

An adapter is an object that makes an existing service meet another interface. An interface is the set of operations and promises callers may use. ScaleAdapter meets Scale by implementing grams. Inside that method it calls the old device, checks its result, and translates the unit. The caller sees grams throughout. The old device does not know that an adapter exists. This is useful at a boundary where two independently developed pieces already disagree.

slides.title: What the C++ mechanism does
keyPoints: The colon in class ScaleAdapter final : public Scale declares public inheritance: the adapter may be used wherever a Scale is required.
At compilation, the compiler checks that light_enough may call grams through const Scale&.
ScaleAdapter also contains a reference, device_.
slides.narration:
The colon in class ScaleAdapter final : public Scale declares public inheritance: the adapter may be used wherever a Scale is required. This is a type relationship, not a statement that the adapter owns a Scale object. The inherited pure virtual function, marked = 0 in Scale, demands an implementation. The override word asks the compiler to check that grams matches it, including its final const. A misspelled name or missing const produces a compile error instead of a hidden new method. final prevents further derivation; this example does not need another layer of subclasses.

At compilation, the compiler checks that light_enough may call grams through const Scale&. At execution, virtual dispatch selects ScaleAdapter::grams for our actual object. The ampersand makes scale a reference, so the function borrows the existing object rather than copying it. const prevents that call from modifying the object through this interface. It does not prove the physical sensor never changes. Here the simulated device stores one fixed reading, making our printed results repeatable.

ScaleAdapter also contains a reference, device_. Its constructor stores a connection to a LegacyScale that already exists. No device copy is made; no allocation is needed. The caller must keep that device alive for every adapter call. main creates device first and scale second. Local objects are destroyed in reverse order, so the adapter goes away before the device. Destroying the adapter does not destroy the borrowed device. Scale has a virtual destructor so a future owner holding a base-class pointer can destroy a derived adapter correctly.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch06.json → Units and errors are part of the contract
slides.title: Units and errors are part of the contract
keyPoints: A boundary must translate meanings, not just names.
Dividing two integers discards the fractional part.
The contract assumes nonnegative integer milligrams are valid readings and all negatives signal failure.
slides.narration:
A boundary must translate meanings, not just names. In grams(), raw is checked before conversion. The value -1 is an error marker, not negative physical weight. Throwing std::runtime_error ends the normal call, so light_enough cannot accidentally accept the parcel. The error reaches the test's matching catch block. The adapter leaves both itself and its device unchanged when the call fails.

Dividing two integers discards the fractional part. Writing 1000.0 makes the divisor a double; the integer is converted for floating-point division. The returned double represents grams. This does not make floating-point arithmetic exact for every fraction. The test therefore uses a small tolerance when checking 1.25. The exact boundary values used here, two and zero, are represented exactly. A measurement system with strict legal or scientific rounding rules would need an explicit rule and perhaps an integer base unit throughout.

The contract assumes nonnegative integer milligrams are valid readings and all negatives signal failure. Real devices may distinguish timeout, overload, and calibration errors. An adapter should preserve distinctions the application needs instead of flattening every failure into zero. It should also avoid inventing precision: dividing an integer milligram count does not create a more precise measurement.

slides.title: Composition and multiple inheritance
keyPoints: C++ also permits a class to inherit from two bases.
Our object adapter uses composition in the broad design sense of holding a connection to another object.
When debugging an adapter, write down three things before changing code: the input unit and error range, the target unit and error contract, and the lifetime owner.
slides.narration:
C++ also permits a class to inherit from two bases. A class adapter could inherit from Scale and LegacyScale, then use the inherited milligrams member. That approach may fit a legacy class designed for derivation, especially when overriding its virtual behavior is necessary. However, the adapter then contains its own legacy base subobject. It cannot automatically wrap the device instance that the application already owns. Public inheritance from the legacy type can also expose operations the new interface was meant to hide.

Our object adapter uses composition in the broad design sense of holding a connection to another object. The connection is borrowing, so the diagram uses a dependency arrow rather than an ownership diamond. It keeps lifetime policy with main and permits several adapters to view one device when that is intended. If the adapter should control the device's lifetime, a value member or unique_ptr would state a different ownership rule. Choose that rule from the actual device lifecycle, not from the pattern's name.

When debugging an adapter, write down three things before changing code: the input unit and error range, the target unit and error contract, and the lifetime owner. A wrong answer can come from any of them. When replacing a device library, keep the parcel tests unchanged and add device-specific adapter tests. That small boundary limits how far vendor changes travel through the program.

question.prompt: Why keep light_enough independent of LegacyScale?
question.answer: Its rule is about grams and a Scale contract. Keeping the old device API outside the client makes replacement devices easier to integrate and test.

slides.title: Two different relationships in one object
keyPoints: ScaleAdapter implements Scale.
device_ refers to a separate LegacyScale.
An inheritance arrow does not mean ownership.
slides.narration: Read the two relationships separately. Public inheritance says that a ScaleAdapter may serve as a Scale. Its grams operation must therefore keep the Scale promise. The device_ member says something else: this adapter remembers an existing LegacyScale. Because the member is a reference, it is a connection to that same object, not another device copy. The UML triangle points toward the interface being implemented. The dependency toward LegacyScale represents use and borrowing. Neither line claims that the adapter deletes the device. If these facts are mixed together, a reader may invent a destructor that destroys something the adapter never owned.
actions: Trace the inheritance arrow and the dependency separately.

question.prompt: Who owns the LegacyScale in the chapter program?
question.answer: main owns the local LegacyScale. The adapter borrows it and must not delete it.

theory.what: One type promise plus one stored borrowed connection.
theory.where: ScaleAdapter derives from Scale and stores device_.
theory.why: The old instance already exists and must meet a new caller contract.
theory.invariant: A successful call returns grams, and the device remains alive.
theory.risk: Confusing borrowing with owning can cause invalid deletion or dangling access.

slides.title: The compiler checks the call shape
keyPoints: virtual selects an implementation at runtime.
override checks the complete promised signature.
const constrains access; it does not freeze a sensor.
slides.narration: The compiler knows that a const Scale reference supports grams. The pure virtual declaration ends in equals zero, which requires concrete implementations to provide that operation. ScaleAdapter writes override so the compiler checks that its spelling, parameters, and const qualification match. At runtime, the actual object selects ScaleAdapter's body even though the client speaks through Scale. The const after the function parameters says that this call does not modify the object through its ordinary members. It does not prove that a physical sensor is frozen or that repeated readings always agree. Our simulated device happens to store a fixed integer.
actions: Compare the two grams signatures character by character.
Predict what removing const from the overriding signature would do.

question.prompt: Can override prove that grams returns the correct physical unit?
question.answer: No. It checks the virtual signature. Unit meaning remains a documented and tested contract.

theory.what: A checked interface call selects the concrete implementation.
theory.why: Clients remain independent of the particular device type.
theory.invariant: The override matches the interface and honors its meaning.
theory.risk: A perfectly matched signature can still return milligrams by mistake.

slides.title: Read once, validate once, translate once
keyPoints: Keep the raw reading in a local value.
Reject all negatives before conversion.
An exception prevents a parcel decision.
slides.narration: Follow one call from the client's point of view. It asks for grams. The adapter obtains one raw reading and stores it locally. That matters for a real sensor because two reads might produce different results. The adapter validates the exact value it later converts. If the value is negative, throwing transfers control to a matching handler; light_enough never gets a number to compare. If the value is valid, division changes the unit and returns a new value. This order forms a small transaction: either the caller gets a valid measurement or it gets a failure. Returning zero on error would break that agreement.
actions: Trace 1250 and -20 through the same three operations.

question.prompt: Why is testing only raw == -1 weaker than raw < 0 here?
question.answer: The stated device contract treats every negative reading as failure, including -20.

theory.what: A boundary translates the success and failure meanings together.
theory.where: ScaleAdapter::grams before it returns to light_enough.
theory.why: A status marker must never become a successful measurement.
theory.invariant: The checked reading is the converted reading.
theory.risk: Reading again after validation can use an unchecked measurement.

slides.title: A reference does not keep its source alive
keyPoints: Construct the device before the adapter.
Destroy the adapter before its device.
Choose an owning member only when ownership is required.
slides.narration: Borrowing is cheap because it does not create a new owner. That advantage comes with a rule: the borrowed device must still exist whenever the adapter uses it. In main, construction order is device and then adapter. Local destruction happens in reverse order, which fits the rule. Returning an adapter that refers to a function's local device would break it after that function returns. Do not run that invalid design to see what happens; access through the dead reference would have undefined behavior. If the adapter must control device lifetime, redesign construction to receive an owning value or unique_ptr instead of pretending a reference owns anything.
actions: Draw overlapping lifetime bars for main, device, and adapter.

question.prompt: Does a const reference member extend the lifetime of an arbitrary local device?
question.answer: No. Its owner must keep that device alive for every later adapter call.

theory.what: The adapter stores access without storing ownership.
theory.where: The device_ reference member and constructor initializer.
theory.why: The application already controls this device instance.
theory.invariant: No adapter use occurs after the device is destroyed.
theory.risk: A returned adapter can retain a reference to a dead local object.

slides.title: Calibration is a separate design decision
keyPoints: The lab subtracts a finite nonnegative offset.
Reject a negative adjusted result.
A shared calibration wrapper may suit many scale types.
slides.narration: The extension adds calibration, which means adjusting a measurement using an agreed offset. The solution validates the offset once during construction and validates each adjusted reading during the call. These are different checks because configuration and device readings arrive at different times. Clamping a negative adjusted result to zero would hide a problem that the stated lab requires us to reject. There is also a design choice. If calibration belongs specifically to this device integration, storing it in the adapter is reasonable. If many unrelated scales need the same adjustable behavior, a separate Scale wrapper could reuse that policy. Explain the change boundary before selecting either design.
actions: Compare device 1250 with offsets 0.25, 1.25, and 2.0.

question.prompt: Why validate that the offset is finite as well as nonnegative?
question.answer: NaN and infinity do not represent usable finite calibration amounts; a sign check alone does not reject every such value.

question.prompt: Explain Adapter without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together. A free conversion function is simpler if all callers can use it. A multiple-inheritance adapter can reuse protected legacy behavior but ties the adapter to a legacy base subobject and its construction rules.

slides.title: Choose the smallest truthful boundary
keyPoints: One call site can use a helper.
An existing object contract can justify Adapter.
Multiple inheritance wraps a base subobject, not an arbitrary instance.
slides.narration: Suppose a teammate asks whether every conversion deserves an adapter class. The answer depends on the caller. A script that reads one value can use our first helper. Existing code that requires a Scale needs an object that satisfies that contract. A class adapter using multiple inheritance is another option, but it changes the object arrangement: the legacy base is part of the adapter itself. It does not automatically wrap the already-existing device in main. These are meaningful alternatives, not levels of sophistication. Select the one whose interface and lifetime match the requirement, and write down the constraint that made it necessary.
actions: Ask pairs to argue for a helper in a one-file script and an adapter in a device plugin.

question.prompt: What question distinguishes the helper solution from the adapter solution?
question.answer: Must this service be usable through an existing Scale object interface, or does the caller only need a converted number?

slides.title: Diagnose the symptom before editing the class
keyPoints: Wrong fractions: inspect operand types.
Failure accepted: inspect error translation.
Unstable crashes: inspect lifetime and ownership.
slides.narration: Three reports can look like one vague complaint that the adapter is broken. A result of one for 1999 points toward integer division. A failed device reported as light enough points toward missing validation. A crash after leaving a setup function points toward a stored reference whose source has died. These clues suggest different investigations. First reproduce the symptom with the smallest valid test, then follow the value or lifetime that can cause it. A useful repair keeps the original client rule unchanged and adds a targeted boundary test. Avoid rewriting the whole abstraction until the evidence identifies a structural problem.
actions: Give each group one symptom and ask for the first two lines they would inspect.

question.prompt: Which regression cases catch unit loss and the parcel threshold together?
question.answer: Test a fractional reading such as 1250, exactly 2000, and 2001, then separately test negative error readings.

slides.title: Say Adapter without naming a class
keyPoints: An existing service and caller disagree.
One boundary translates operations and meaning.
Preserve errors, units, and lifetime rules.
slides.narration: Close your source window and explain the pattern using only the parcel story. The caller speaks grams. The old service speaks milligrams and negative status values. A small object presents the caller's contract, makes the old call, and translates the answer without hiding failure. That is the full reasoning path from problem to mechanism. Now transfer it to a clock API that reports seconds while an application expects milliseconds. The arithmetic changes, but the questions remain: what are the units, what signals failure, who owns the underlying service, and what can the unchanged caller safely assume? Remembering those questions is more useful than memorizing a box diagram alone.
actions: Have learners explain the clock variation in sixty seconds without reading notes.

question.prompt: What must an adapter preserve beyond a compatible function name?
question.answer: The required value meaning, failure behavior, and safe access to the adapted service.

graph.title: A new contract around an old device
graph.caption: The hollow triangle points from adapter to Scale. Dashed dependencies mean use, not ownership. light_enough calls grams; the adapter reads raw milligrams, checks the error range, and returns grams. Teaching panels describe those operations and are not extra UML edges.
